description: We’re developing an AI-native space mission game that combines immersive storytelling, engaging gameplay mechanics, and a variety of interactive features inspired by real space missions. We’re really excited about this project and its potential! We’re currently looking for passionate team members with experience in game development or UI/UX design to help bring our vision to life.
summary:
Ares: First Light is a strategy game where players run a space programme from Mars and win by establishing a colony on all eight planets, including floating platforms on the gas and ice giants.
The game addresses the Space Mission Design challenge by putting players in charge of decisions that can make or break a mission. They choose a spacecraft’s power supply, shielding, landing system, and antenna to suit its destination. For supported Earth departures, the game calculates launch windows using JPL planetary data supplied with NASA’s GMAT and checks payload capacity against Atlas V 401 performance data. Players also write software rules that let a spacecraft respond to trouble before instructions arrive from home, which is a unique feature of our game. 
A guided first mission explains the science behind each choice. Players can see why a mission failed, revise their design, and try again. That makes concepts like launch windows, communication delays, and fault protection tangible for learners in space engineering for the first time.
The project also includes aspects of the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, where players manage resources and build colonies under adverse conditions. The challenging nature of the missions makes the gameplay exciting for new players. The modular design of the game allows for other intended uses: a teacher making their own lessons using our game framework. The futuristic AI assistant Jarvis helps the player to complete their missions.
details:
Ares: First Light is a browser-based strategy game we developed for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players run a space programme from Mars and follow each mission from the drawing board to a working base on another world. The goal is to establish a colony on all eight planets. The guided first mission asks players to design a lander for Earth. Later missions take them to destinations as different as the surface of Venus, the cloud layers of Neptune, and etc. The campaign spans several years in three-month turns, with a limited budget that changes according to the programme’s results.

How a mission works

In the Shipyard, players choose an objective, hull, engine, trajectory, payload, launch vehicle, and propellant load. They then configure six spacecraft systems: power, thermal control, radiation shielding, landing equipment, hull strength, and antenna. A rotatable 3D model shows the spacecraft as they modify it. Every addition has a consequence. A pressure-resistant hull can protect a Venus lander, but its extra mass leaves less capacity for payload or propellant. Waiting for a better launch window may save fuel while delaying supplies that a base needs.

Players also write software rules for fault protection. Radio signals can take minutes or hours to reach a distant spacecraft, so it must be able to react to danger on its own. In our first mission, an Earth lander can encounter a hurricane near its landing site. The player can program the rule “WHEN wind speed is above 55 FOR 1 turn THEN descend to a calmer layer.” In the simulation, descending protects the instruments but reduces solar power for that turn. A test run shows what the sensors detected, when the rule fired, and how the battery responded. Players can diagnose a failure and revise their software before launch. Other worlds introduce different dangers, including dust storms and solar flares on Mars.

Our creative contribution

We connected spacecraft design, programmable fault protection, and a 3D-style isometric surface so that the same engineering decision matters at several stages of play. After landing, players scan terrain and choose where to build. An ice deposit can supply a water plant. That water can support a greenhouse, feed oxygen production, or become propellant for the next spacecraft. Elevation and terrain affect construction and production, so the landscape itself helps players reason about where a base should grow. Rocky worlds have surface settlements, while the four giant planets have fictional robotic cloud platforms. A launch is therefore both the outcome of one design problem and the beginning of another.

Scientific consistency and educational impact

We use the same scientific relationships when teaching a concept, checking a design, and explaining its outcome. For Earth departures to Mercury, Venus, Mars, and Europa, we calculated launch windows and launch energy from JPL planetary positions distributed with NASA’s General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). Atlas V 401 performance data sets the launch mass limit, and the rocket equation checks whether the spacecraft has enough propellant to brake on arrival. Destination checks combine NASA planetary facts about distance, temperature, gravity, and pressure with simplified ratings for radiation hazards and equipment. A student can learn why sunlight weakens with distance, see a solar-powered design struggle at Saturn, change the power source, and test that prediction.

We also drew on Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for crew survival and Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data for the problem of growing food with limited resources. Players manage food, water, oxygen, energy, and shielding, prepare for forecast hazards, ship supplies between bases, and build research labs to unlock technologies such as more efficient greenhouses. Our intended impact is for students to be able to explain why a mission succeeded or failed and choose what to change on the next attempt. The tutorial explains the science behind each choice. AURA, our offline advisor, flags urgent problems, while JARVIS, powered by Google Gemini, answers questions such as “Why did my mission fail?” using the player’s current campaign.

Tools and design considerations

We used Python 3 for game rules and simulations and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interface, maps, and spacecraft visualization. We used GitHub for collaboration, Render for hosting, and FFmpeg to prepare the planetary soundtrack. Players can use a computer or phone without specialized hardware. We considered accessibility through keyboard controls and reduced-motion support, and we balanced scientific accuracy with playability by labeling estimated routes, fictional hazards, and simplified production values. Varying hazards and arrival conditions give players a reason to test their assumptions and carry reserves, even when a design performed well on an earlier mission.
